'''''Osmanthus fragrans''''' ({{Literal translation|fragrant [[osmanthus]]}}) is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Oleaceae]].<ref name=POWO>{{cite web |url= https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:610878-1 |title= Osmanthus fragrans Lour. |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=The Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=July 15, 2025}}</ref><ref name=COL>{{cite web |url= https://www.catalogueoflife.org/data/taxon/74ZQZ |title= Osmanthus fragrans Lour. |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Catalogue of Life |publisher=Species 2000 |access-date=July 15, 2025}}</ref> In English, it is sometimes referred to by the common names '''sweet osmanthus''', '''sweet olive''', '''tea olive''', and '''fragrant olive'''. It is native to [[Assam]], Cambodia, China, the [[Himalayas]], [[Hainan]], Japan, Myanmar, Taiwan, Nepal, Thailand, and Vietnam.<ref name=POWO/> In China it grows in the provinces of [[Guizhou]], [[Sichuan]], Hainan, and [[Yunnan]].<ref name=foc>Flora of China: [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=210001392 ''Osmanthus fragrans'']</ref><ref name=fop>Flora of [[Pakistan]]: [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=5&taxon_id=210001392 ''Osmanthus fragrans'']</ref><ref>[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=354988 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families, ''Osmanthus fragrans'']</ref><ref>[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/653228#page/47/mode/1up Loureiro, João de. 1790. ora Cochinchinensis 1: 29, ''Osmanthus fragrans'']</ref>

In China, it is the "city flower" of the cities of [[Hangzhou]], [[Zhejiang]]; [[Suzhou]], [[Jiangsu]]; and [[Guilin]], [[Guangxi]]. In Japan, it is the "city tree" of [[Kitanagoya]], [[Aichi Prefecture]]; [[Kashima, Saga|Kashima]], [[Saga Prefecture]]; [[Beppu]], [[Ōita Prefecture]]; and the "town tree" of [[Yoshitomi, Fukuoka|Yoshitomi]], [[Fukuoka Prefecture]].

==Etymology==
The genus name ''Osmanthus'' is composed of two Greek etymons: ''osma'' meaning "smell" and ''anthos'' meaning "flower".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Evans |first=Linsay |date=2021-07-29 |title=Osmanthus Flower Meaning and Symbolism |url=https://www.petalrepublic.com/osmanthus-flower/ |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=Petal Republic |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Dehgan |first=Bijan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=stu3EAAAQBAJ |title=Garden Plants Taxonomy: Volume 2: Angiosperms (Eudicots) |date=2023-04-05 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-031-11565-3 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Gledhill |first=D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NJ6PyhVuecwC |title=The Names of Plants |date=2008-03-06 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-86645-3 |language=en}}</ref> The specific name ''fragrans'' is a borrowing from the Latin meaning "odorous, fragrant" referring to the intense fragrance of its flowers.

==Growth==
It is an [[evergreen]] [[shrub]] or small tree growing to {{convert|3–12|m|abbr=on}} tall. The leaves are {{convert|7–15|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2.6–5|cm|abbr=on}} broad, with an entire or finely toothed margin. The flowers are white, pale yellow, yellow, or orange-yellow, small, about {{convert|1|cm|abbr=on}} long, with a four-lobed [[Corolla (botany)|corolla]] {{convert|5|mm|abbr=on}} diameter, and have a strong fragrance; they are produced in small clusters in the late summer and autumn. The fruit is a purple-black [[drupe]] {{convert|10–15|mm|abbr=on}} long containing a single hard-shelled seed; it is mature in the spring about six months after flowering.<ref name="foc" /><ref name="fop" /><ref name="mitomori">Mitomori: [http://www.mitomori.co.jp/hanazukan/hanazukan2.6.47kinmo.html ''Osmanthus fragrans''] (in Japanese; [https://translate.google.com/translate?hl=en&sl=ja&u=http://www.mitomori.co.jp/hanazukan/hanazukan2.6.47kinmo.html&sa=X&oi=translate& google translation])</ref><ref name="rhs">Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. Macmillan {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}.</ref>

==Cultivation==
It is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] in [[East Asian gardens]],<ref>{{cite journal |title=China Through the European Nose|author=Xuelei Huang |page=6 |journal=ICS Bulletin |date=Dec 2023 |issue=4  |publisher=Institute of Chinese Studies, [[Chinese University of Hong Kong]]|url=https://www.ics.cuhk.edu.hk/images/ICS_Bulletin/ics_bulletin_2023_no4_eng.pdf}}</ref> and gardens in Europe, North America, Australia and elsewhere in the world for its deliciously fragrant flowers which carry the scent of ripe [[peach]]es or [[apricot]]s.<ref name=rhs/> A number of [[cultivar]]s have been selected for garden use, with varying flower colors, such as ''Osmanthus fragrans'' 'Yanhua' with its variegated foliage and orange blooms.<ref name=foc/><ref name=rhs/> Within Japan, the white- and orange-blossoming subspecies are distinguished as ''ginmokusei'' (<small>lit.</small> "silver osmanthus") and ''kinmokusei'' (<small>lit.</small> "gold osmanthus"), respectively.{{Cn|date=March 2021}}

==Uses==

===Culinary===
In [[Chinese cuisine]], its flowers may be infused with [[green tea|green]] or [[black tea]] leaves to create osmanthus tea ({{zh|c=桂花茶|p=guìhuāchá|labels=no}}). The flowers are also used to produce osmanthus-scented jam, [[osmanthus cake]]s, dumplings, soups, and [[osmanthus wine|osmanthus liquor]]. Osmanthus jam is used as an ingredient in a type of [[gruel]] called ''[[chátāng]]'', which is made from [[sorghum]] or [[millet]] flour and sugar mixed with boiling water.  This dish is associated with the northern city of [[Tianjin]], although it may also be found in [[Beijing]].{{Cn|date=March 2021}}

Osmanthus is also used for making many traditional Chinese desserts, such as osmanthus [[tangyuan (food)|tangyuan]] with [[Jiuniang|rice wine syrup]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.teas.com.au/blogs/tea-recipes/osmanthus-rice-wine-syrup-tong-yuan|title = Osmanthus Tong Yuan with Rice Wine Syrup 桂花酒釀湯圓| date=23 February 2019 }}</ref>

===Repellent===
In some regions of northern India, especially in the state of [[Uttarakhand]], the flowers of sweet osmanthus are used to protect clothes from insects.<ref name="ref00vafob">[https://books.google.com/books?id=ibXvAAAAMAAJ A manual of Indian timbers: an account of the growth, distribution, and uses of the trees and shrubs of India and Ceylon, with descriptions of their wood-structure], James Sykes Gamble, S. Low, Marston & Co, 1922, ''... Osmanthus, Lour ... A very sweet scented tree, the flowers having the scent of apricots. These flowers are used in China to flavour tea and in Kumaon to protect clothes from insects ...''</ref>

===Medicinal===
In [[traditional Chinese medicine]], osmanthus tea has been used as an [[herbal tea]] for the treatment of [[irregular menstruation]].<ref>Zhou S.,"Flower herbal tea used for treatment of menopathies".,  ''Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine'' 2008 28:3 (202–204)</ref> The extract of dried flowers showed neuroprotective, free-radical scavenging, [[antioxidative]] effects in ''[[in vitro]]'' assays.<ref>Lee H.-H., Lin C.-T., Yang L.-L. "Neuroprotection and free radical scavenging effects of Osmanthus fragrans.",  Journal of Biomedical Science 2007 14:6 (819–827)</ref>

== Cultural associations ==
[[File:Osmanthus Fragrans chinese Guihua.JPG|thumb|left|''Osmanthus fragrans'' in full bloom (October) in [[Jingjiang]], China]]
From the occasion of its blossoming, the sweet osmanthus is closely associated with the Chinese [[Mid-Autumn Festival]]. [[Osmanthus wine]] is a traditional choice for the "reunion wine" drunk with one's family, and osmanthus-flavored confections and teas may also be consumed. [[Chinese mythology]] held that a sweet osmanthus grows on the moon and was endlessly cut by [[Wu Gang]]:{{NoteTag|The tree was originally identified as a {{lang|zh|{{linktext|桂}}}} (''guì'') and described in the terms of the osmanthus.<!-- sources at [[Wu Gang]] --> However, in English, it is often associated with the more well-known [[Chinese cassia|cassia]] (''Cinnamomum cassia'', now known in Chinese as the {{lang|zh|{{linktext|肉桂}}}} or "meat ''gui''"); while, in Chinese, it has instead become associated with the Mediterranean [[bay laurel|laurel]], which is now known as the {{lang|zh|{{linktext|月桂}}}} or "Moon ''gui''", from the similar associations of victory and success.}} some versions held that he was forced to cut it every 1000 years lest its luxuriant growth overshadow the moon itself, others that he was obliged to cut it constantly only to see it regrow an equal amount every day.<ref name=wolfman>Eberhard, Wolfram. ''Dictionary of Chinese Symbols: Hidden Symbols in Chinese Life and Thought'', [https://books.google.com/books?id=Ul8kVMexa6gC&pg=PA76 pp. 76 ff]. Routledge & Kegan Paul (London), 2013. Accessed 12 November 2013.</ref>

In late [[imperial China]], the osmanthus was also associated with the [[imperial examination]]s, which were held in the 8th lunar month. The ''[[chengyu]]'' "pluck osmanthus in the [[moon toad|Toad]] Palace" was a refined paraphrase for "passing the exam",<ref name="moooon">Brendon, Juliet & al. ''The Moon Year: A Record of Chinese Customs and Festivals'', [https://books.google.com/books?id=3vUZMgM5bhQC&pg=PA410 p. 410]. Kelly & Walsh, 1927. Reprinted Routledge (Abingdon), 2011. Accessed 13 November 2013.</ref><ref>Zdic. "[http://www.zdic.net/c/e/a7/196726.htm {{lang|zh|蟾宫折桂}}]". 2013. Accessed 13 November 2013. {{in lang|zh}}</ref><ref>{{lang|zh|杜近芳}} [Du Jinfang]. [http://tieba.baidu.com/p/84960300?pn=2 {{lang|zh-Hans|《红楼梦汉英习语词典》}}] ["A Dictionary of Chinese Idioms in the ''[[Dream of the Red Chamber]]''"]. 2003. Accessed 13 November 2013. {{in lang|en}} & {{in lang|zh}}</ref> in part since one would attract hangers-on as if he smelled as sweet as osmanthus thereafter.<ref name="wolfman" /> "Breaking the osmanthus twig and mounting the dragon" was another [[Chinese euphemisms|euphemism]], in this case, for [[sex in China|sex]].<ref name="wolfman" />
